title: Juniper Networks Certified Associate Junos (JNCIA-Junos JN0-105)

nodes.title: Part 1: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Part 1. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: Which two software components of the Junos OS architecture are separated to ensure that control-plane churn cannot interrupt forwarding of transit packets?
flashcards.back: Junos OS is built on a strict separation between the Routing Engine (RE), which runs the protocols and owns the master copy of the configuration, and the Packet Forwarding Engine (PFE), which forwards transit traffic against a downloaded forwarding table. Because the PFE keeps forwarding even when the RE is busy or rebooting, control-plane churn does not interrupt user traffic. J-Web and the CLI are both management interfaces sitting on top of the RE, candidate vs rescue configs are two configuration databases on the RE, and syslog/kernel are RE-internal services — none of those pairs describe the control- vs data-plane split.

flashcards.front: You have typed several `set` statements while in configuration mode but have not yet activated them. Which Junos configuration database currently holds those changes?
flashcards.back: Junos uses a candidate configuration as a scratchpad: every `set`, `delete` or `edit` you issue in configuration mode edits this candidate, not the running device. Nothing takes effect until you `commit`, at which point the candidate becomes the new active configuration and the previous active is pushed onto the rollback stack as rollback 1. The rescue configuration is a user-selected snapshot restored with `rollback rescue`, the active configuration is what is currently running, and rollback 0 is the active configuration itself (the file you just committed).

flashcards.front: Which Junos command applies the staged candidate configuration but reverts it automatically after 10 minutes unless a follow-up command is issued?
flashcards.back: `commit confirmed <minutes>` activates the candidate immediately but starts a timer; if you do not issue a plain `commit` within that window the device automatically rolls back to the previous configuration. This protects against locking yourself out after a risky change. `commit check` only validates syntax without activating anything, `commit synchronize` pushes the configuration to both Routing Engines on a dual-RE chassis, and `commit and-quit` activates the configuration and leaves configuration mode but provides no auto-revert.

flashcards.front: Which Junos login class permission grants full read-write access to every hierarchy and lets the user execute all commands?
flashcards.back: Junos ships four predefined login classes. `super-user` carries all permission bits (`all`), so a user in that class can both view and modify any hierarchy and execute every operational command. `operator` allows operational-mode tasks such as clearing interfaces but cannot change configuration, `read-only` can only view configuration and operational state, and `unauthorized` cannot log in at all. Custom classes can be built with a subset of permission flags when finer-grained control is needed.

nodes.title: Access control lists: Key Ideas
nodes.content: An ACL is an ordered list of permit/deny rules evaluated top-down until first match. Used everywhere: router interfaces, switch ports, NTFS files, cloud network ACLs. Order matters — a permit at line 5 won't fire if a deny at line 3 matches the same traffic.

flashcards.front: Standard vs extended ACL — what's the difference?
flashcards.back: Standard ACL (Cisco IOS 1-99): matches source IP only. Extended (100-199 or named): matches source IP + destination + protocol + port. Use extended for anything realistic — standard ACLs can't say 'block SSH from this subnet to that host'. Apply extended close to the source, standard close to the destination.

Every ACL has an invisible `deny ip any any` at the end. If nothing matches your permit rules, traffic is dropped. Common gotcha: configure 'permit ssh from 10.0.0.0/24', forget that this blocks DNS, NTP, ICMP — anything you didn't explicitly permit. Always log the implicit deny while testing to see what you accidentally blocked.

flashcards.front: Inbound vs outbound — which direction to apply?
flashcards.back: Inbound: filter traffic ENTERING the interface BEFORE the router routes it. Outbound: filter traffic LEAVING after the router decided where it's going. Inbound is more efficient (drops bad traffic before routing); outbound is rarely needed except for specific egress filtering. When in doubt, apply inbound on the closest interface to the source.

flashcards.front: Why does order matter in an ACL?
flashcards.back: Rules are evaluated top to bottom; first match wins. If you put 'deny 10.0.0.0/24' before 'permit 10.0.0.5', host .5 is denied — its specific permit never gets reached. Order most-specific rules first, broad rules last. Always end with explicit denies that log, so you can see what's getting blocked.

questions.q: On a Juniper MX router an interface is shown as `ge-0/2/3.0`. What does the `.0` at the end of that name represent?
choices: Slot number on the FPC where the PIC is installed
Logical unit (sub-interface) carrying protocol family configuration
questions.explanation: Junos interface names follow `<media>-<fpc>/<pic>/<port>.<unit>`. For `ge-0/2/3.0`, ge is Gigabit Ethernet, 0 is the FPC slot, 2 is the PIC, 3 is the port and the trailing `.0` is the logical unit number. Protocol families (`family inet`, `family inet6`, VLAN tags, MPLS, etc.) are always configured under a unit, not directly on the physical port, so every usable interface needs at least unit 0. Loopback uses `lo0.<unit>`, not the trailing field of a transit interface.

questions.q: A Junos router has learned the same prefix 10.20.0.0/16 from OSPF (route preference 10) and from a static route (route preference 5). Which route is installed in the forwarding table, and why?
choices: The OSPF route, because dynamic protocols always win over static
The static route, because its route preference value is lower
Both routes are installed and traffic is load-balanced 50/50 by default
Neither — Junos rejects the conflict until one source is withdrawn
questions.explanation: Junos selects the route with the lowest route preference (its equivalent of administrative distance). Static routes default to preference 5 and internal OSPF routes default to preference 10, so the static route wins and is installed in the forwarding table; the OSPF route stays as a backup in the routing table marked hidden by the active flag of the static. Load-balancing only happens between routes of equal preference (and equal metric) when `per-packet`/`per-flow` load balancing is enabled via a routing policy.

questions.q: Which statement best describes a stateless firewall filter in Junos OS?
choices: It tracks TCP connection state and only allows return traffic for established sessions
It performs deep packet inspection up through layer 7 of the OSI model
It evaluates each packet independently against `from`/`then` terms based on header fields
It is applied only on the loopback interface to filter Routing Engine traffic
questions.explanation: Junos stateless firewall filters (analogous to ACLs on other platforms) are made of ordered terms, each with `from` match conditions on header fields (addresses, ports, protocol, DSCP, etc.) and a `then` action (`accept`, `discard`, `reject`, `count`, `policer`). Each packet is judged on its own — there is no session table — which is why they are called stateless. Connection tracking, return-flow inspection and L7 inspection are jobs for the SRX stateful security policy, not stateless filters. Stateless filters can be applied on any interface, including the lo0 interface to protect the Routing Engine, but their use is not restricted to lo0.

questions.q: Which Junos OS service is described as a protocol-independent property — meaning it can act on routes regardless of which routing protocol learned them?
choices: BGP attribute manipulation inside a peer group
Routing policy that imports or exports routes between the routing table and protocols
questions.explanation: Junos routing policy and routing options (aggregate, generated, static, martians, autonomous-system) are configured under `[edit routing-options]` and `[edit policy-options]`, and they apply to the routing table regardless of where a route was learned. The same policy framework filters BGP advertisements, OSPF redistribution and static-to-IS-IS leaks alike. OSPF summarization, BGP attribute changes and PIM RP election are all features of specific routing protocols, so they are by definition protocol-dependent, not protocol-independent.

nodes.title: Part 3: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Part 3. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: On a Junos EX Series switch interface configured for trunk mode, which type of frames are sent untagged by default?
flashcards.back: On a Junos trunk port the configured native VLAN (`native-vlan-id` under the interface) is transmitted and accepted untagged, while every other VLAN carried on the trunk is 802.1Q-tagged. This matches the IEEE 802.1Q behaviour used by other vendors and lets a trunk interoperate with hosts or legacy switches that do not tag. The native VLAN is configurable per port (not fixed to VLAN 1), broadcast/multicast frames are tagged according to the VLAN they belong to, and saying that everything is always tagged would defeat the purpose of having a native VLAN.

flashcards.front: Which operational-mode command displays a summary of every interface on a Junos device along with its admin and link status?
flashcards.back: `show interfaces terse` is the go-to one-line-per-interface summary in operational mode: it prints the interface name, admin status, link status, and any configured protocol families with their addresses. `show configuration interfaces` shows configured statements, not live status. `monitor traffic interface` is the Junos tcpdump-equivalent used to capture transit packets. `request system halt` shuts the device down — a destructive command that has nothing to do with viewing interface status.

flashcards.front: How many forwarding classes does Junos OS support by default, and what is each one mapped to in the Class-of-Service framework?
flashcards.back: Out of the box Junos defines four forwarding classes — best-effort, expedited-forwarding, assured-forwarding, and network-control — each mapped to one of four output queues (0 through 3) on the egress interface. You can extend the model (up to 8 or 16 queues depending on the platform) but the default four-class, four-queue layout is what JNCIA-Junos expects you to know. The two- and zero-class options are simply wrong, and mapping every class to the same queue would defeat the purpose of differentiated service.

flashcards.front: After committing a configuration that you suspect broke OSPF, which Junos command returns the device to the configuration that was active immediately before that commit?
flashcards.back: Junos keeps the previous active configurations on a numbered rollback stack — rollback 0 is the current active, rollback 1 is the one immediately before it, up to rollback 49 on most platforms. Entering configuration mode and typing `rollback 1` loads that previous configuration into the candidate; you then `commit` to make it active. `load override terminal` reads a brand-new configuration from your paste buffer (not from history), `request system reboot` restarts the device (which would simply reload the broken active config), and `clear ospf neighbor all` only resets OSPF adjacencies without reversing the configuration change.

questions.q: On a Junos EX Series switch interface configured for trunk mode, which type of frames are sent untagged by default?
choices: Frames belonging to the configured native VLAN ID
All multicast and broadcast frames regardless of VLAN
Only frames in VLAN 1 (which cannot be changed)
No frames — every frame on a trunk port is always 802.1Q tagged
questions.explanation: On a Junos trunk port the configured native VLAN (`native-vlan-id` under the interface) is transmitted and accepted untagged, while every other VLAN carried on the trunk is 802.1Q-tagged. choices: Two forwarding classes, mapped to two output queues (high and low priority)
Four forwarding classes (best-effort, expedited-forwarding, assured-forwarding, network-control), each mapped to its own queue
Eight forwarding classes, all mapped to a single shared queue and prioritized purely by DSCP
Zero — forwarding classes do not exist until you configure a custom CoS profile
